html:
The big picture

A program describes the solution to a problem precisely enough for a computer to execute it: an algorithm (the steps) working on data (Wirth: algorithms + data structures = programs). How the program text reaches the hardware depends on the language: it is compiled ahead of time, interpreted step by step at run time, or — like Python — first compiled to bytecode that a virtual machine then interprets. The data live in main memory, and a variable is a named cell there whose data type decides how its bit pattern is read and what you may do with it. The steps themselves are built from very few pieces: assignment, sequence, branching, repetition and subroutines — and Böhm & Jacopini showed that sequence, branching and repetition already suffice for anything computable. The Nim game at the start and end shows all of it working together.

Connection

Much of this lecture revisits the prep course with more precision: algorithms, flowcharts and compiled vs interpreted languages in 1 Algorithms, Flowcharts and Programming Languages, Python's bytecode step in 2 Python, and variables and data types in 3 Variables. New here: the memory model behind variables, the formal properties of an algorithm, the Böhm–Jacopini result and Nassi–Shneiderman diagrams.

What is »programming«?

Describing the solution to a problem in a sufficiently precise way that it can be executed by a computer.

A program is

  • a sequence of commands or instructions that
  • processes a set of data.

Niklaus Wirth: ALGORITHMS + DATA STRUCTURES = PROGRAMS

Intuition

Wirth's formula splits every program into two questions: what are the steps? (the algorithm) and how is the information organised? (the data structures). This lecture introduces both halves in their simplest form — single variables for the data, the five kinds of statements for the steps. The rest of the course grows each half.

A first problem: the »Nim« game

From a pile of matches, two players take turns to take away 1 to (for example) 3 matches, the one who takes the last match being the winner.

Program invocation: python3 NIM.py

A game against the program (17 matches, 1–3 per move, the computer starts):

We play with 17 matches – 1-3 must be taken away at a time.
I start.
||||| ||||| ||||| ||
I take 1 matches.
||||| ||||| ||||| |
Your move (1-3): 3
||||| ||||| |||
I take 1 matches.
||||| ||||| ||
Your move (1-3): 3
||||| ||||
I take 1 matches.
||||| |||
Your move (1-3): 3
|||||
I take 1 matches.
||||

|
I take 1 matches.
I won.

We will learn to understand the program in the next course units. (The algorithm itself is at the end of this note.)

What happens (in principle)? Interpreted and compiled languages

These details are for orientation only.

Compiled languages (C, C++, …)

  1. The compiler analyzes the source code (*.c, *.cpp) and translates it into native machine code for a specific target platform (»object code« *.o, *.obj).
  2. The linker combines object files and binds external references to program libraries, creating a standalone executable program.
  3. The loader copies the executable into main memory and transfers CPU control to the program's entry point.

Scheme: source code → native machine code → direct execution by the CPU. (Steps 1–2 happen at compile time, step 3 at runtime.)

Interpreted languages (Bash, Tcl, awk, …)

The interpreter analyzes and executes the source code directly at runtime, typically instruction by instruction. There is usually no separate compilation step that produces a standalone executable program.

Scheme: source code → execution by an interpretation program.

Example: compilation vs. interpretation

You find a Latin recipe (Mustacei — Farinae siligineae modium unum musto conspargito…) and want to try it out…

Solution I (compiler):

  • We ask a Roman (≙ compiler) to translate the whole recipe into English (compilation) — we do this once for each new recipe.
  • We give the translated recipe (Cider breads — Sprinkle must on a bushel of wheat flour…) to a cook (≙ CPU, execution) — each time we want to prepare the dish.

Solution II (interpreter):

  • We find a Roman (≙ interpreter) who tells the cook (≙ CPU), step by step, what to do (analysis and execution go hand in hand) — each time we want to prepare the dish.
Why does anyone still compile, if interpreting is so convenient?

Look at where the translation work happens in the recipe story. The compiler pays the translation cost once; every later run is pure cooking at full speed. The interpreter pays it every time, while the cook waits — slower, but you can change the recipe and try it again immediately, and the same recipe works with any cook who has a Roman at hand (portability).

So the trade-off is speed of execution (compiled) against flexibility and portability (interpreted). Hybrid languages, next, try to get part of both.

Hybrid languages (Python, Java, …)

  1. A compiler analyzes the source code (e.g., *.py) and compiles it into an intermediate code (»bytecode«). Bytecode is a low-level, platform-independent representation of the program. In Python, source files (*.py) are compiled to Python bytecode, which may be stored in .pyc files in the __pycache__ directory.
  2. A platform-specific runtime system executes the bytecode. Python bytecode is executed by the Python interpreter / Python virtual machine.

Thus, hybrid languages combine compilation and interpretation.

Scheme: source code → bytecode → execution by a virtual machine or interpreter.

How a program reaches the hardware

Compiled: translated before execution. Interpreted: executed step by step by an interpreter. Hybrid: compiled to bytecode, then executed by a VM.

Common mistake — "Python is an interpreted language, so nothing is compiled"

Python is usually called interpreted, and that's why the claim sounds right. But the diagram's third column shows what really happens: the source is compiled to bytecode first, and only the bytecode is interpreted. What Python does not produce is native machine code or a standalone executable — that's the real difference from C. The same question came up in the prep course: 2 Python.

Data

ALGORITHMS + DATA STRUCTURES = PROGRAMS

The data that we process is located in the so-called main memory and is accessed (read or written) by the central processing unit (CPU), consisting of the arithmetic-logic unit (ALU), the control unit (CU), and registers (fast memory cells):

Input devices → I/O processor ↔ CPU (ALU, CU, registers) ↔ memory; output devices.

  • The data are binary coded (0/1). Depending on the coding rule we can store integers, rational numbers, letters, etc.
  • Individual cells of the main or random access memory (RAM) are addressed as variables in the program.
  • Our simplified memory model: a vertical table of bytes (where each row may consist of so many bytes that the value shown can be stored in it), e.g. cells holding 4711, 3.1415926, 0, 'M', 'H'.

(The commands are also stored in the main memory → »von Neumann architecture«.)

Source: John von Neumann, First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC (1945). In: IEEE Annals of the History of Computing, Vol. 15, Issue 4, 1993.

Intuition — why "commands are also stored in memory" matters

In a von Neumann machine the program is just more data sitting in RAM. That's what lets a computer run any program you load, and it's also why a compiler or interpreter can exist at all: they are programs that read program text as data and produce or execute other instructions.

Variables in higher programming languages (classical model)

A variable is a named »data container«, with

  • address (position in memory) – corresponds to its identifier (name);
  • type or data type (category) – defines the allowed values, the size in memory, as well as the supported operations;
  • value (content) – may change during the course of the program (»at run time«). It is binary coded: 17_{10} = 10001_2 — consisting of bits, bytes (8 bits), words (2–8 bytes).

Memory model (»classical«, non-Python) — on the stack (part of the computer's main memory): the name (identifier) x labels the cell at address 2256120, whose content is 4711 (the data type of x is integer = a whole number); the neighbouring cells have the addresses 2256116 and 2256124.

The Python memory model will be introduced soon.

Riddle: What is the size of variable x (in bytes), if this is the memory of a computer with 1-byte machine words?

What's the answer to the riddle?

4 bytes. With 1-byte machine words, every byte has its own address. The cells shown start at 2256116, 2256120, 2256124 — each 4 addresses apart. So x occupies the 4 bytes 2256120 to 2256123, and the next variable starts at 2256124.

Worked example — reading a binary value

Goal: check the slide's 17_{10} = 10001_2.

  1. Write the place values of the 5 binary digits, from the right: 16, 8, 4, 2, 1.
  2. Keep those with a 1: 10001_2 has 1s at 16 and 1.
  3. Add them: 16 + 1 = 17. ✓

The same method gives 01000011_2 = 64 + 2 + 1 = 67 — a number you'll meet again on the data type slide.

Relatives of variables in higher programming languages

Literal — a data value that appears in the program text without a variable name (but may be »packed« into an invisible variable by the compiler), e.g., a number: 5 or 3.6, or a text: "This is a text literal".

Constant — a variable whose content cannot be changed, e.g., PI for 3.141592653589793… Other features are shared with the notion of a variable (address, data type, name – for constants).

Connection — constants in Python

Python has no keyword that makes a variable unchangeable. By convention, a name written in capitals (PI = 3.14159, MAX_TAKE = 3) means "treat this as a constant" — but Python won't stop you from reassigning it. The Nim program's max_take is exactly the kind of value that would be such a constant.

Data type — the key to making sense of the bit pattern in memory

All data have a type (»are of type …«, e.g., »integers«), which

  • defines the interpretation of the code stored in memory. An element of a data type (e.g., 5) is called a value or an instance. Creating a data element of a given type is called instantiating (the type).
  • defines the value range, e.g., −32768 .. 32767
  • … and thus, the memory requirements (e.g., 2 bytes)
  • defines the allowed operations, e.g., +, -, *, /, =, <, >
  • restricts the use of the data: x + "A" (forbidden because meaningless, if the type of x is numeric) → helps to avoid erroneous nonsensical use → type safety

Example (content shown in binary; the slide writes L for 1): at addresses 4122313 and 4122314 both x and y contain the bit pattern 0L0000LL. The data type of x is integer → whole number 67; the data type of y is character → C.

In Python, the data type of a variable can change in the course of the program. We can check the current type: type(variable). In many other languages (Java, C, C++ …, especially the compiled languages), the data type of a variable is fixed and must be specified at the point of definition.

Why do x and y hold the same bits but different values?

Memory stores only bits; it has no idea what they mean. 0L0000LL = 01000011_2 = 67. Read as an integer, that is 67. Read as a character, the computer looks up code 67 in a character table — and in ASCII (and Unicode) code 67 is the letter C. The type is the only thing that decides which reading applies — hence "the key to make sense of the bit pattern".

Why does a range of −32768 .. 32767 go with 2 bytes?

2 bytes = 16 bits, and 16 bits have 2^{16} = 65536 different patterns. Splitting them evenly around zero gives 2^{15} = 32768 negative values (-32768 \dots -1) and 32768 non-negative ones (0 \dots 32767). One more bit doubles the range; that's why the type determines both the range and the memory size.

Connection

Type safety in practice: in Python, 5 + "A" stops with a TypeError. The prep course's 3 Variables covers this and the casting functions int(), float(), str().

Algorithm

Algorithm := precise, step-by-step instructions for solving a problem. (Cf. assembly instructions for do-it-yourself furniture, cooking recipes, directions from a route planner…)

Etymology: Muhammad ibn Musa Al-Chwarizmi (latinized Algorismi), 780–859, astronomer and mathematician from Baghdad. 825 A.D.: first textbook on the rules of arithmetic using the decimal system originating in India (basic arithmetic operations). → »Algorithm«

ALGORITHMS + DATA STRUCTURES = PROGRAMS

Properties

Different sources come up with different property sets… (cf. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algorithm_characterizations)

Properties that a procedural description should satisfy to be called an algorithm:

  • An algorithm must be unambiguously describable in a finite text (finiteness). This description is based on a certain »processor type« (computational model, e.g., human, von Neumann computer, Turing machine, quantum computer, …).
  • Each step must be executable on that »processor type« (executability).
  • It may require only a finite amount of memory at any given time (dynamic finiteness).
  • It may require only a finite number of steps (termination).

In practice, there are often additional restrictions:

  • The algorithm must produce the same result under the same conditions (determinacy).
  • The next step to be applied must be uniquely defined at each point in time (determinism).
Intuition — telling the six apart
  • Finiteness is about the text: the recipe fits on a page.
  • Dynamic finiteness and termination are about the run: at no moment do you need infinite storage, and the run eventually stops.
  • Executability means every step is something the processor can actually do ("add two numbers" yes, "find the best move" no, unless you say how).
  • Determinacy is about the result (same input → same output); determinism is about the path (at every point there is exactly one next step).

A deterministic algorithm is always determinate, but not the other way round: an algorithm can take a random path and still always reach the same result.

Common mistake — "a random program can't be an algorithm"

The Nim program flips a coin to decide who starts and sometimes takes a random number of matches. So it is neither determinate nor deterministic — yet it satisfies all four core properties (finite text, executable steps, finite memory, it terminates because matches only decrease). Determinacy and determinism are the slide's additional, practical restrictions, not part of the definition.

Instructions and statements

Instructions control the processor – the instruction set for machine programs depends on the processor type, e.g. (here: hypothetical machine language):

InstructionMeaning
LDA 10load 10 into the accumulator register
MUL 6multiply the content of the accumulator register by 6
ADD 7increase the content of the accumulator register by 7
STA xstore the content of the accumulator register in the memory cell with address x

Together these four instructions compute x ← 10 * 6 + 7.

In a high-level programming language, the instructions (statements, commands) are independent of the processor type. The most important ones are:

  • Evaluation of expressions (calculations) and value assignment (e.g. x ← 10 * 6 + 7)
  • Command sequence* (compound statement, composite statement, sequence)
  • Branching* (conditional statement, selection, choice) – two-way or multiway
  • Loop* (iteration, repetition) – head-controlled or foot-controlled
  • Subroutine call
  • Jump statement (struck through on the slide)

*Böhm & Jacopini (1966): "Everything that is in principle computable can be computed with command sequence, (two-way) branching and repetition."

Corrado Böhm & Giuseppe Jacopini: Flow diagrams, Turing machines and languages with only two formation rules. CACM 9, 5 (1966), 366–371.

Why is the jump statement crossed out, if machine languages are full of jumps?

At the machine level, branches and loops are built from jumps ("if the accumulator is 0, continue at address 120"). Böhm & Jacopini showed that a high-level language doesn't need a free jump (goto) at all: sequence, branching and repetition can express every computable procedure. Programs built only from these blocks read top to bottom, each block with one entry and one exit, which makes them far easier to follow and check. That's the "structured" in structured programming — and the course title.

Value assignment

The figure shows the standard model. The Python memory model will be introduced soon.

x ← 10 * 6 + 7

  • Assigns the value of the expression on the right side (r-value; to the right of the assignment symbol ←) to the variable on the left side (l-value, here: x) after its evaluation (here: 67). The variable stores the value until the next assignment.
  • An earlier content of the variable is overwritten by the assignment.
  • The variable can be used in any calculations after the assignment.

x ← x + 1

  • Changes the value of the variable x
  • Adds 1 to the previous value
  • Assigns the result to x again

(In memory: the cell named x at address 4122314 changes its content — its value — from 67 to 68.)

LanguageNotation
Python (and most other programming languages)x = 10 * 6 + 7
Pascalx := 10 * 6 + 7;

Pascal attempted to avoid the risk of confusion with a mathematical equation.

Common mistake — reading = as "equals"

As an equation, x = x + 1 has no solution. As an assignment it is perfectly sensible: first evaluate the right side with the old value of x, then store the result in x. The arrow ← and Pascal's := both show this direction. In Python, "is equal to" is written == — see 2 Python.

Worked example — tracing assignments

Predict the final values, then check the trace:

a ← 5
b ← a * 2
a ← a + b
StepWhat happensab
1store 5 in a5—
2read a (5), compute 10, store in b510
3read a and b (5 + 10), overwrite a1510

Rule: the right side always uses the values at that moment; b does not change when a changes later.

Command sequence

Consecutive execution of several statements:

StatementsExample
Statement 1x ← 3
Statement 2y ← 4
…z ← x + y
Statement k

After the example: x = 3, y = 4, z = 7.

  • Graphical notation: Nassi–Shneiderman diagram (structogram) — simple rectangular instruction blocks, nested if necessary.
  • Graphical notation: flow chart (flow diagram) — statements are connected by arrows representing the flow of control.
  • Optional assertion: statement about the state of the algorithm at a certain point (here: x = 3, y = 4, z = 7).

Command sequences also allow their statements to be logically combined into a unit that can be treated as a single statement in a greater context.

Intuition — two ways to draw the same thing

A flowchart shows the path the computer takes (arrows). A structogram shows the nesting (boxes inside boxes) and has no arrows at all — so it can't draw a free jump, which is exactly what structured programming wants. You know flowcharts from 1 Algorithms, Flowcharts and Programming Languages; the Nim algorithm below is a structogram.

Branchings

Two-way branching — selection of the next statement(s) based on a logical expression.

Structogram: a header Condition? splits into a yes column (Statement_yes) and a no column (Statement_no).

Example — the minimum of two numbers:

x < y ?
  yes: min ← x
  no:  min ← y

Afterwards (assertion): min = minimum of x and y. (In the flowchart, the yes branch is labelled x < y and the no branch x \ge y.)

Multiway branching — selection of the next statement(s) based on an expression with a finite value range: value = ? selects Statement_1 (1st value), …, Statement_n, or Statement_otherwise.

Why does the assertion "min = minimum of x and y" hold for sure?

Check both branches. If x < y, the smaller one is x, and the yes branch stores x. Otherwise x \ge y, so y is the smaller (or they're equal, and either is right), and the no branch stores y. Every possible input goes through exactly one branch, and both leave the correct value — that's how you argue an assertion is true.

Repetition

Head-controlled loop — repeat as long as a condition checked at the loop entry is fulfilled.

n ← 0
While x > 1
    x ← x / 2
    n ← n + 1

After the loop (assertion): x \le 1 \land n = \lceil \log_2 x_0 \rceil, where x_0 is the starting value of x.

Symbols
  • \land — logical "and": both conditions hold
  • x_0 — the value x had before the loop; n — the loop counter (number of halvings)
  • \log_2 x_0 — the power of 2 that gives x_0 (how many times you can halve x_0 before reaching 1)
  • \lceil \cdot \rceil — ceiling: round up to the next whole number

Foot-controlled loop — repeat as long as a condition checked at the loop exit is fulfilled (structogram: Statement with While … underneath).

Unclear (slide 25)

The assertion under the flowchart reads "x ≤ 1 ∧ n = log₂ x₀" with a gap around the logarithm; ceiling brackets were most likely lost there. \log_2 x_0 alone is wrong whenever x_0 isn't a power of 2 (for x_0 = 20 the loop runs 5 times, while \log_2 20 \approx 4.32). The note writes \lceil \log_2 x_0 \rceil, which holds for every x_0 \ge 1.

Worked example — tracing the halving loop

Start: x_0 = 20, n = 0.

Check x > 1?x after halvingn
20 > 1 yes101
10 > 1 yes52
5 > 1 yes2.53
2.5 > 1 yes1.254
1.25 > 1 yes0.6255
0.625 > 1 no → leave loop

Check the assertion: x = 0.625 \le 1 ✓, and \lceil \log_2 20 \rceil = \lceil 4.32 \rceil = 5 = n ✓. So the loop counts how many halvings it takes to get down to 1.

Common mistake — head- and foot-controlled loops run the same number of times

A head-controlled loop may run zero times: start with x_0 = 0.5 and the condition fails immediately, so n stays 0. A foot-controlled loop checks only after the body, so it always runs at least once. Python's while is head-controlled; Python has no built-in foot-controlled loop.

Subroutines

Parts of a program can also be formulated elsewhere as a subroutine (subprogram), where the control flow

  • branches there if required (call), possibly transporting data (arguments) into the subroutine and
  • returns to the place of the call after the subroutine has terminated (return), possibly yielding a result.

We use subroutines to

  • factor out common parts of an algorithm for reuse
  • structure larger programs in »digestible units« (modules)

Example: a program has one statement that needs m! and later one that needs k!. Both call the same subroutine — once with n ← m, once with n ← k — and get back m! and k!:

Factorial (IN n)
    fac ← 1
    for i ← 2 to n
        fac ← fac × i
    Result ← fac

Some special types of subroutines (in Python also called »function«):

  • Functions: compute a value from given arguments (like Factorial(n))
  • Procedures: produce a certain effect (e.g., print something on the screen), but do not return a value
  • Methods: used to implement operations on data types, e.g., "John F. Kennedy".find(' ') (→ 4) — a text string, and the call of method find() for that text string
Worked example — calling Factorial(4)
  1. Pass the argument: n ← 4.
  2. Initialise: fac ← 1.
  3. Loop i = 2, 3, 4: fac becomes 1 \cdot 2 = 2, then 2 \cdot 3 = 6, then 6 \cdot 4 = 24.
  4. Return 24 to the place of the call.

Why does the loop start at 2? Multiplying by 1 changes nothing, so starting at 2 saves a step. And Factorial(0) and Factorial(1) still come out as 1: the loop simply doesn't run.

Intuition — why find(' ') gives 4

Positions in a string are counted from 0: J=0, o=1, h=2, n=3, space=4. So the first space is at position 4. Python counts list positions the same way (4 Lists & Loops).

The »Nim« game as an algorithm

Part 1: Preparation

matches ← 17                    # e.g.
max_take ← 3                    # e.g.
"We play …"                     # Output
comp_turn ← Random(True, False) # »Flip coin«
comp_turn?
  yes: "I start"
  no:  "You start"

The slide labels the parts: matches is a variable, 17 a literal, text after # a comment. A bare text like "I start" is short for the command "output 'I start' on the console window".

Part 2: Game

The game loop as a Nassi–Shneiderman diagram.

The same algorithm as indented pseudocode:

While matches > 0                        # As long as matches are still in play
    Output matches
    comp_turn?
      yes: matches ≤ max_take?
             yes: take ← matches         # all
             no:  take ← matches mod (max_take + 1)
                  take = 0?
                    yes: take ← Random(1..max_take)
      no:  take ← User input
    "I take … matches"
    matches ← matches – take
    comp_turn ← ¬ comp_turn              # Players take turns
comp_turn?
  yes: "You won"
  no:  "I won"
Why does the computer take matches mod (max_take + 1)?

With a maximum of 3 per move, whatever you take (1, 2 or 3), I can always take the rest to 4 (3 → 1, 2 → 2, 1 → 3). So if I leave you a multiple of 4, I can keep it that way every round: 16 → 12 → 8 → 4 → 0, and I take the last match.

matches mod 4 is exactly how many I must take to reach the next multiple of 4 below. From 17 that's 1, which is why the computer took 1 match every time in the game on slide 10. If matches mod 4 is 0, I'm already on a multiple of 4 myself: no winning move exists, so the program takes a random number and hopes you make a mistake.

Why does "comp_turn? yes" at the end mean you won?

The last statement in the loop flips comp_turn. So when the loop ends, comp_turn says who would move next, not who moved last. If it's the computer's turn now, you took the last match — "You won". In the slide 10 game the computer took the last match, the flag flipped to no, and the output was "I won".
